stories.title: Scottsdale Schwab Offices Undergoing $11.7M Revamp
stories.excerpt: Charles Schwab Corp. is investing millions into an extensive renovation of a nearly 84,000-square-foot office space in north Scottsdale where the firm is planning a major Arizona expansion. The Dallas Business Journal reports the financing services company filed a permit for $11.7 million in tenant improvements at the Two Scottsdale Landing office complex at 8701 E. Hartford Drive off Pima and Bell roads. The Class B, Two Scottsdale Landing office complex is adjacent to the 124-acre Mack Innovation Park, where Toy Barn is working toward developing its largest luxury car storage facility and electric vehicle maker Rivian is opening its first Scottsdale service and repair facility. It’s also near the future site of Taser maker Axon Enterprise Inc.’s massive headquarters project. Dallas-based Schwab is one of the largest financial companies in the U.S. with more than $13 trillion in assets under management. bullets: Charles Schwab investing $11.7M to renovate 84,000-sq-ft office in north Scottsdale
Expansion signals major financial services employment growth in Phoenix metro

stories.summary: Charles Schwab is undertaking an $11.7 million tenant improvement project at Two Scottsdale Landing office complex in north Scottsdale as part of a major Arizona expansion. The Dallas-based financial services giant, managing $13 trillion in assets, is positioning itself in a rapidly densifying innovation corridor anchored by Axon Enterprise headquarters, Rivian's Scottsdale service facility, and Mack Innovation Park. The company's capital deployment signals confidence in Arizona's white-collar job growth and talent retention.
stories.impact: Schwab's major office expansion and capital commitment to north Scottsdale signals incoming corporate employment growth that will drive sustained rental demand in Phoenix metro multifamily. The clustering of high-wage employers (Axon, Rivian, Schwab) in the Innovation District submarket creates a talent magnet effect that will support premium apartment rents and occupancy in adjacent residential submarkets through 2026–27, particularly for luxury and Class A product serving finance, tech, and automotive sectors.

stories.title: Suburban Office Leads U.S. Pricing Gains in June
stories.excerpt: Led by suburban office properties, U.S. commercial property prices moved higher in June, with the RCA CPPI US National All Property Index rising 0.9% from a year earlier, MSCI Real Assets reported. The index gained 0.7% in the second quarter from Q1, implying a faster annualized growth pace of 2.6%. “Borrowing costs in the U.S. appear anchored at an elevated level, with the Federal Reserve holding its policy rate steady under new chairman Kevin Warsh,” reported MSCI Real Assets. Despite this, office prices continued rising in June, with suburban prices posting annual growth of 3.0%. While CBD office prices rose at the same monthly pace as their suburban counterparts, CBD pricing remains 50% below its March 20922 peak, a sharper drawdown than the 15% gap seen in suburban assets. Retail prices fell 0.1% from a year earlier in the sixth consecutive monthly decline, reflecting the sharper monthly drops in Q4 2025 more than current conditions. Industrial prices turned negative on an annual basis in June, falling 0.4%, down from a recent peak rate of 7.5% in June 2024. Apartment prices fell 1.7% in June from a year earlier, the 10th consecutive month of annual declines. The index dropped 1.2% from Q1, a change that annualizes to a more pronounced decline of 4.8%. The post Suburban Office Leads U.S. Pricing Gains in June appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Apartment prices fell 1.7% annually in June, 10th consecutive month of declines
Industrial prices turned negative, down 0.4% annually; retail fell 0.1%
CBD office fell 50% from March 2022 peak; suburban office +3.0% annual growth
stories.summary: U.S. commercial real estate prices rose 0.9% annually in June per MSCI CPPI, driven by suburban office (3.0% annual growth), though apartment prices continued declining for the tenth straight month, falling 1.7% year-over-year. Industrial prices turned negative at –0.4% annually after peaking at 7.5% growth in June 2024. CBD office remains 50% below its March 2022 peak, while suburban office has recovered more resilience, suggesting a structural bifurcation in office demand and value retention.
stories.impact: The sustained 10-month decline in apartment prices signals slowing velocity and persistent oversupply in many markets despite strong absolute demand—a red flag for development feasibility. Rising cap rates and negative annual price momentum in industrial also constrain alternative uses for apartment sites. Developers should focus on supply-constrained submarkets and flight-to-quality dynamics where Class A rents and occupancy remain resilient; avoid oversupplied secondary markets and commoditized product.

stories.title: Vornado Foresees $350-per-Foot Rents at Park Avenue Office Tower: Earnings
stories.excerpt: Vornado Realty Trust announced Tuesday morning that it could levy as much as $350 per square foot at one of its latest office developments, at a time when rents over $300 a square foot at trophy properties are becoming the norm. 350 Park Avenue, which Vornado is developing with Ken Griffin’s Citadel and Rudin, may be renting for $350 per square foot, and Roth said he has confidence the building will still see leasing due to lack of supply and strong demand in the Class A office market. The news came during Vornado’s second-quarter earnings call. One investor on the call, after adding up all investments in the structure, asked for confirmation that Vornado would start asking rent at $350 and up, which Vornado Chairman Steven Roth confirmed as accurate. “The fact that there’s a scarcity of new supply, and the combination of the construction costs, interest rates, et cetera, require a very high rent for a new building,” Roth said. “That will cause the great, well-located, older buildings to go up and drive [leasing] enormously. And obviously, that’s the reason we bought Park Avenue Plaza.” Vornado began developing the property at the end of the fourth quarter of 2025, aiming for 1.85 million square feet of office. During the earnings call, Vornado reported that net income decreased to $16.4 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $743.8 million over the same period in 2025, despite strong performance elsewhere on its balance sheet. Funds from operations (FFO), however, reached $144 million in the second quarter, compared to $120.9 million year-over-year. Revenue saw an increase as well, rising to $462.2 million in the three months ending June 30, in contrast to $441.4 million in the second quarter of 2025. Vornado attributed the slide in net income to an $803.2 million master lease of 770 Broadway to New York University, but executives and investors on the call did not seem fazed by that individual metric. bullets: Vornado's 350 Park Ave (with Citadel, Rudin) targeting $350/sq-ft rents in NYC

stories.summary: Vornado Realty Trust announced it will ask $350 per square foot for 350 Park Avenue, a new Manhattan office development co-owned with Citadel and Rudin, during its Q2 earnings call. CEO Steven Roth attributed the high rent to construction costs, interest rates, and limited supply of new Class A office space. He predicted that lack of new supply and strong tenant demand will sustain high rents and create spillover demand for well-located older buildings.
stories.impact: Vornado's $350/sq-ft asking rent at a trophy Manhattan office tower signals that construction cost inflation and capital scarcity have permanently raised the development threshold in prime markets. This dynamic will suppress new office supply and create a scarcity premium that props up rents in existing, well-located buildings—but also reinforces the multifamily-office trade-off in urban cores: capital devoted to high-rent office development starves apartment investment, reducing multifamily supply and supporting rent growth in secondary markets and suburban flight-to-quality submarkets nationwide.

stories.title: The Decisions That Changed Everything
stories.excerpt: People often ask me what the secret was to building a business that sold more than three times the number of investment properties than any other firm in New York City for 14 consecutive years. They expect the answer to involve a particular strategy, a recruiting philosophy or some proprietary marketing technique. The truth is much simpler. When I look back over more than four decades in commercial real estate, I don’t believe my career was built by thousands of decisions. It was built by a handful. Most days were ordinary. I showed up, worked hard, made calls, met clients, negotiated transactions and tried to improve a little each day. But, every so often, a decision came along that permanently altered the direction of everything that followed. Those are the moments that shape careers, companies and, ultimately, lives. The first came before my career even began. As a student at Wharton, I thought I wanted to become an investment banker. That was the prestigious path. Then I spent a summer at Coldwell Banker in commercial real estate. I loved the entrepreneurial nature of the business, the direct connection between effort and results, and the opportunity to build relationships rather than simply analyze transactions. I returned the next two summers and joined Coldwell Banker full time after graduation in 1984. Looking back, that single decision determined the course of the next 42 years (and counting). A few years later, Paul Massey and I decided we wanted to start our own company. We walked into Chemical Bank seeking a loan to finance our dream. They laughed at us. No one wanted to lend money to two young brokers with little more than ambition. Instead of abandoning the idea, we spent the next two years saving every dollar we could. By November 1988, we had accumulated $400,000 and launched Massey Knakal. At the time, it felt like an enormous leap into the unknown. stories.title: Urban Standard Capital Grows $200M Credit Facility With Western Alliance Bank
stories.excerpt: Urban Standard Capital has deepened its relationship with a major Arizona bank. Commercial Observer can first report that Urban Standard Capital has increased its aggregate financing capacity for transitional commercial real estate loans with Western Alliance Bank — a Phoenix-based regional bank with $90 billion of assets — to $200 million through three separate funds. The two lenders began their business relationship in 2020. Seth Weissman, founder and managing partner at Urban Standard Capital, a New York-based CRE private credit firm, told CO that the coordinated lending capacity has steadily increased from $40 million to $125 million over the last six years. He added that he expects the credit facility to continue to aid his firm in making loan originations to sponsors for tailored financing projects, which have typically fallen into the $15 million to $20 million range. “It’s a capital partnership that allows us to lower our cost of capital and be able to be more flexible and service our clients better,” said Weissman. “It helps me to deliver speed and flexibility to our borrowers and increases our capacity for lending.” Weissman could not estimate a number of loans the credit facility will ultimately provide, as he noted that the facility recycles each time previous loans pay off. “If I invest $200 million, and a loan pays off for $20 million, I can draw that money again, and I’ll probably turn this money over four times, so it’s probably $800 million of lending power over the life of the arrangement,” said Weissmann. Since beginning its business in 2014, Urban Standard Capital has originated $2.3 billion in loans for more than 260 real estate projects. “That progression didn’t happen overnight,” said Weissman. “It was earned through consistent performance, disciplined underwriting, and delivering on what we said we would do.” Ian Hawk, New York market manager for Western Alliance Bank, noted in a statement that his firm has “built a strong relationship”
bullets: Urban Standard Capital expanded $200M credit facility with Western Alliance Bank
Capacity increased from $40M to $200M over six years; typical loans $15M–$20M
Arizona regional bank (Western Alliance, $90B assets) deepening commitment to CRE credit
stories.summary: Urban Standard Capital, a New York-based CRE private credit firm, increased its aggregate financing capacity for transitional commercial real estate loans with Western Alliance Bank (Phoenix, $90 billion in assets) to $200 million across three separate funds. The facility has grown from $40 million six years ago to $125 million and now $200 million, with typical loan sizes in the $15–$20 million range. Founder Seth Weissman cited lower cost of capital and flexibility as key benefits of the deepened partnership.
stories.impact: Western Alliance Bank's aggressive expansion of transitional CRE lending capacity signals regional confidence in multifamily value-add and repositioning deals across Western and Southwestern markets. The $200M facility underscores strong secondary capital availability for stressed or transitional assets, which improves deal feasibility for sponsors pursuing hold-and-stabilize or light-value-add strategies in secondary metros where traditional bridge debt may be scarce or expensive. This capital depth supports distressed acquisitions and workout scenarios in high-supply markets.

stories.title: Hines Reveals Plans for SouthPark Mixed-Use Venture
stories.excerpt: Hines has plans for a mixed-use development called The Gallery, which will include a 250,000-square-foot office tower; a 19-story, 302-unit multifamily tower; and 50,000 square feet of retail use. The project in SouthPark will replace a single-story retail building at 6601 and 6555 Carnegie Blvd., which currently houses three food-and-beverage purveyors. The Charlotte Business Journal reports the ground-floor retail will surround a plaza that opens up to the street and the multifamily tower will be within walking distance to neighborhood amenities like Symphony Park and The Specialty Shops. Office tower amenities will include private terraces, a shared sky terrace and lounge, conference and training facilities, fitness offerings and direct access to ground-floor retail. JLL’s John Ball, Karah Tanneberger and Claiborne Mulhern will lead office leasing efforts. Hines will handle retail leasing. Hines is developing the site in partnership with Harris Land Co., which owns the property. Hines does not yet have a timeline for construction. stories.summary: Hines is developing The Gallery, a mixed-use project in Charlotte's SouthPark neighborhood, featuring a 302-unit, 19-story multifamily tower, 250,000-square-foot office tower, and 50,000 square feet of ground-floor retail. The project will replace a single-story building housing three food-and-beverage tenants at 6601 and 6555 Carnegie Boulevard. Hines is partnering with Harris Land Co. (property owner); JLL will lead office leasing. No construction timeline has been disclosed.
stories.impact: Hines' SouthPark mixed-use development signals sustained confidence in Charlotte's submarket growth and mixed-use absorption, particularly in affluent, lifestyle-oriented neighborhoods. The 302-unit component captures upscale demand near entertainment and retail; the office and retail towers will compete with existing Charlotte downtown and office parks, but the integrated model suggests strong walkability demand. This project supports Charlotte as a tier-1 multifamily growth market, though development pace remains slow (no start date), indicating land constraints and/or entitlement/financing delays—monitor Charlotte supply pipeline for rent growth opportunities.

stories.title: JV Building 382 Apartment Units in Charlotte’s Innovation District
stories.excerpt: GMH Communities (GMH), in partnership with AEW Capital Management (AEW), completed land acquisition for the development of a 20-story, 382-unit luxury residential mixed-use tower, ANOVA The Pearl, located within The Pearl innovation district in Charlotte, North Carolina. The property is anticipated to open for occupancy in Summer 2028. Located at the intersection of South McDowell Street and Pearl Park Way, ANOVA The Pearl will encompass 1.3 acres within The Pearl and feature luxury residential accommodations, along with 6,621 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Of the 382 units, 5% will be reserved for affordable housing. Residents will have access to an extensive amenity package, including a fitness center, clubhouse, golf simulator and wellness-focused sauna and cryotherapy chambers. On its website, AEW says it has over 800 clients globally, with $85.5 billion in assets under management across all property types in North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. stories.summary: GMH Communities, partnering with AEW Capital Management (which manages $85.5 billion across North America, Europe, and Asia-Pacific), has completed land acquisition for ANOVA The Pearl, a 382-unit luxury residential tower in Charlotte's Pearl innovation district. The 20-story mixed-use project is anticipated to open Summer 2028 and will include 6,621 square feet of ground-floor retail, 5% affordable housing set-aside, and premium amenities targeting affluent tenants. The site spans 1.3 acres at the intersection of South McDowell and Pearl Park Way.
stories.impact: GMH/AEW's entry into Charlotte's Pearl innovation district with a 382-unit luxury tower opening Summer 2028 signals strong institutional conviction in Charlotte's tech and professional services job growth. The 2028 opening timeline aligns with Hines' Gallery (also no start date) and reflects Charlotte's emerging position as a tier-1 multifamily market, but the two large 300+ unit luxury projects suggest rapid supply growth. Developers should monitor Pearl district absorption and rent trajectory post-opening; expect occupancy competition and pressure on Class A rents in 2028–29 in Charlotte's CBD and innovation submarkets.

stories.title: Commercial Real Estate Deal Platform Duxre Launches AI Brief
stories.excerpt: Duxre, a commercial real estate deal platform, announced Tuesday that it has launched AI Brief, a software system that converts unstructured sales and leasing data into a readable large language model (LLM) format. Founded in 2020, Santa Monica, Calif.-based Duxre is a subscription platform that aims to streamline data for CRE brokers to enhance transaction volume and client interaction. AI Brief converts the unstructured files into Markdown files, which are more efficiently readable by LLMs such as ChatGPT and Claude, according to the company. The result, the company says, reduces file size from 50 megabytes down to between 30 and 40 kilobytes, speeds up processing, and minimizes errors. “AI Brief specifically came from what we were seeing as we marketed assets for sale, and what our peers were realizing as they marketed assets for lease,” said Sean Fulp, founder and CEO of Duxre, as well as a vice chair at Colliers. (The two companies are not connected.) “Our deliverables, which are mainly in the form of a PDF, are being put into ChatGPT or Claude to analyze those deals. In the case of an offering memorandum — which can be 60 to 80 pages, and 15 to 20 megabytes in size — the first reader is no longer human, which these documents are created for. “There’s no sophisticated pipeline built for our industry for these documents to have an evaluation system in place to make sure that what’s pulled out of it is accurate. What we’ve been seeing is that the LLMs take these documents and are embellishing and hallucinating, causing issues with our process,” Fulp added. “These LLMs come back to tenants or buyers or brokers with a very convincing output, even if it’s wrong. You could say that the bid-ask spread just gets wider because of the disinformation.” AI Brief works in three ways, Fulp explained: It begins with multi-source ingestion, where the brief is built from everything in the deal file, not just one document. stories.title: 2026 Power Investors
stories.excerpt: “It ain’t about how hard ya hit. It’s about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward,” boxer Rocky Balboa once wisely said. In the past year, there have been plenty of one-two punches for real estate and plenty of scenarios where investors had to have fast feet in order to bob and weave (and occasionally duck). In the original “Rocky” movie — now 50 years old — a little- known Philly fighter goes head to head with the heavyweight champion of the world, putting himself at significant risk in his quest for significant glory. With higher-yielding opportunities an increasing focus for many today, CO’s Power Investors occasionally have a similar conundrum when weighing the risk-reward tradeoff. But they also have the competitive advantage of several years of training, hard work and experience to know when to lean in and punch, and when to leave the ring. This list, now in its second year, features the most powerful investors or investment teams in real estate from 25 different entities. Power is the strength to act, and whether market conditions are favorable or choppy as heck, these investors consistently show up and find savvy ways to generate real returns on behalf of their own investors. While high-conviction themes are a recurring North Star — with housing and logistics continuing to be de rigueur — several investors on the list are busy far from the madding crowd and focused instead on more niche asset classes like manufactured housing, industrial outdoor storage or cold storage. A lot of distress still exists in the system and the bid-ask spat is ongoing, but our investors aren’t fazed by market dislocation or bumps. Instead, they’re leaning into it and maximizing the market opportunity for however long that window lasts.
